findings.title: Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
findings.body: Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(codes))` (setup.ts) and compared by decrypting and `indexOf` here. Backup codes are password-equivalent second-factor secrets; storing them in a reversibly encrypted blob means a DB dump plus the (often co-located) CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY yields plaintext second factors for every user. They should be hashed individually (e.g. bcrypt/argon2) and compared by hash, as is done for passwords.

findings.title: Backup code login unusable for non-CAL identity providers
findings.body: For users whose identityProvider is GOOGLE/SAML, 2FA is completed via the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow. In that flow the user submits only `backupCode` with an empty `totpCode`, so the earlier guard at line 113 (`user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode`) throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` before the new backup-code branch is reached. SSO users therefore can never use the "Lost access" backup-code path even though the UI offers it.

findings.title: Consumed backup code replaced by null, leaving holes in array
findings.body: `backupCodes[index] = null` keeps a `null` entry in the stored JSON instead of removing it. Any future code that counts remaining codes, displays them, or validates the array shape must handle nulls; `JSON.parse` of this array also makes `indexOf` semantics depend on nulls never being produced by user input. Filtering the code out (or storing a per-code used flag) would be safer.

findings.title: No rate limiting or brute-force protection on backup-code verification when disabling 2FA
findings.body: The login path calls `checkRateLimitAndThrowError` before verifying credentials, but this endpoint verifies an attacker-supplied `backupCode` against the decrypted code list with no rate limit and no invalidation of failed attempts. With a stolen session cookie plus known password this allows unlimited guessing of 10-char hex codes. Add rate limiting consistent with the login flow.

findings.title: JSON.parse / symmetricDecrypt of backupCodes can throw an unhandled error
findings.body: If `user.backupCodes` was written with a different encryption key or is otherwise corrupt, `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` throws a raw exception that surfaces as a generic 500 rather than a meaningful ErrorCode, breaking login for that user with no diagnostic. Wrap in try/catch and map to `ErrorCode.InternalServerError` (same applies to disable.ts line 58).

findings.title: backupCodes state typed as never[] and blob URL leaked on unmount
findings.body: `useState([])` infers `never[]`, so `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` and `backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode)` are only accepted because the payload is `any`; this silently defeats type checking. Additionally the object URL created with `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked when a new one is created — if the modal unmounts the URL is never revoked, leaking the blob (which contains the plaintext backup codes) for the lifetime of the document. Type the state as `string[]` and revoke the URL in a cleanup effect.

findings.title: No test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
findings.body: The new feature's core behavior (authenticating with a backup code, single-use invalidation, rejecting an already-used or wrong code) is untested; only the backup-code display/download/copy UI is exercised. The TODO acknowledges this. Without a test, regressions in the authorize() backup-code branch would silently allow or block logins.

findings.title: Component exported as `TwoFactor` in BackupCode.tsx
findings.body: The default export in `BackupCode.tsx` is declared as `function TwoFactor(...)`, which is misleading in React devtools/stack traces and confusing for anyone searching for the backup-code component. Rename to `BackupCode`.
